speaker: Tim Latimer
title: Tim Latimer on Solving the Financing Problem for Geothermal
question: In renewable and geothermal power finance, why do rising interest rates disproportionately hurt project economics compared to riskier fossil fuel projects?
guest: As interest rates started to rise, two areas were especially challenged: startups based on long-term growth, and capital-intensive businesses with a lot of capital upfront and a long payback period. That was a double whammy for a capital-intensive startup. Renewable energy projects—solar, wind, and geothermal—are high CapEx with long payback periods, and they have a different profile than other energy infrastructure. All of our projects have 15-year offtake agreements with locked-in pricing, so we don't have to worry five years from now whether the price of our product goes up or down. We also don't have any fuel cost, so we eliminate a lot of volatility. As a result, renewable projects like geothermal have historically been viewed as much safer investments. That's generally good because you can bring lower-cost capital into the space, but it also means your spread off the risk-free rate is a lot tighter than for a fossil fuel project or a project with more risk. When interest rates move, the relative impact for something with a low spread is a lot bigger, hitting renewable infrastructure projects in a big way.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Renewable and geothermal projects are hit harder because their costs are almost entirely upfront capital, while fossil plants spread much of their cost over time as fuel and operating expenses.

A wind, solar, or geothermal plant has essentially no fuel cost, so its levelized cost of energy is dominated by repaying the initial investment (for geothermal, including expensive, risky drilling before any revenue). That capital is typically financed with high leverage, often 70–80% debt, against long-term fixed-price contracts. When rates rise, the financing cost on that large capital base rises directly, and because revenues are fixed under power purchase agreements, the project cannot pass the increase through. Higher discount rates also shrink the present value of cash flows that arrive over 20–30 years.

A gas plant, by contrast, is cheaper to build per unit of capacity, and most of its lifetime cost is fuel bought as it goes, which is largely insensitive to interest rates and often passed through in power prices. Its higher risk premium also means the base rate is a smaller share of its total cost of capital.

As a rough illustration, analyses by the IEA and Wood Mackenzie suggest a two-percentage-point rate rise lifts renewable LCOE by about 20%, versus roughly 11% for gas.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer: Rising interest rates hit renewable and geothermal projects disproportionately hard because of their front-loaded costs, long payback horizons, and high debt leverage. Unlike fossil fuel plants, which require less upfront capital and incur most lifetime expenses gradually through ongoing fuel purchases, solar, wind, and geothermal facilities spend nearly everything upfront, followed by decades of near-zero fuel costs. Geothermal is especially exposed due to costly early-stage drilling and multi-year development timelines that accrue financing charges well before generation begins. Consequently, the cost of capital dominates clean energy’s levelized cost of electricity. Moreover, because contracted clean power projects carry low operational risk once built, developers finance them with high debt-to-equity ratios backed by multi-decade, fixed-price power purchase agreements whose bond-like cash flows lose significant present value as discount rates rise and cannot easily reprice upward. By contrast, riskier fossil fuel projects rely more heavily on equity, already embed steep risk premiums—making a base-rate hike a smaller proportional jump in total financing cost—and target shorter payback periods with merchant revenues that often rise alongside inflation.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Rising rates hurt renewables and geothermal more because of how their costs are structured, not because they are riskier. Most of their lifetime cost is paid upfront: turbines, panels, drilling and wells, and plant construction. Fuel is free, and operating costs are low. That makes the cost of capital the largest driver of their levelized cost of electricity. Financing often makes up half or more of it, which is why studies by the IEA and others find that a few points on the interest rate can raise renewable LCOE by 20–40%.

Fossil plants spend a much larger share of their lifetime cost on fuel, which is paid as they go and doesn't depend on interest rates. Higher rates therefore change their total cost less, even though they carry more market and fuel-price risk. Renewable projects also rely on high leverage and long-dated debt to reach their low tariffs. Many sell power under fixed-price contracts, so they can't pass higher financing costs on to buyers. Geothermal is hit especially hard because the expensive, risky drilling happens before any revenue comes in, often years earlier, so its construction capital costs the most to carry.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer:
Renewable and geothermal power projects are disproportionately hurt by rising interest rates because their costs are heavily front-loaded. Unlike fossil fuel plants, where a large share of lifetime expenses comes from ongoing fuel purchases, renewables and geothermal require nearly all spending upfront as capital expenditure for equipment or drilling, with minimal operating costs afterward. Because almost the entire lifetime cost of generation must be financed at the outset, higher borrowing rates inflate their levelized cost of electricity far more sharply than for gas or coal plants.

These projects also behave like long-duration bonds. Their predictable output encourages high debt leverage and multi-decade, fixed-price power purchase agreements. When rates rise, higher discount rates steeply erode the present value of distant cash flows, while fixed contracts prevent developers from passing financing costs to buyers. Riskier fossil fuel projects typically use less debt, pay back faster, and can pass fuel and inflation costs through to power prices.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Rising interest rates hit many renewable and geothermal projects harder because more of their lifetime cost is paid before they sell any electricity. Wind and solar pay for equipment and construction up front, while geothermal also has to fund exploration and drilling. These projects then generate power for decades with little or no fuel expense. Higher rates make the upfront investment more expensive to finance and reduce the present value of the electricity sales that repay it. If the project has already signed a fixed-price power purchase agreement, it may have little room to pass on the added cost.

A gas-fired plant typically spends less up front per unit of capacity and pays more of its lifetime costs as it buys fuel. That makes its cost per unit of electricity less sensitive to financing rates, even if lenders charge it a higher risk premium. The distinction is between how risky a project is and how much its economics depend on the cost of capital.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Wind, solar, and geothermal plants incur most of their costs before they sell any electricity. They need little or no purchased fuel, so much of their economic value comes from decades of low operating costs. Higher interest rates make construction debt more expensive and reduce the present value of those future savings. Geothermal projects can be especially exposed because developers may finance years of exploration and drilling before revenue begins.

Risk and interest-rate sensitivity are different. A gas-fired plant may face greater fuel-price risk while requiring less capital upfront. Much of its spending occurs later, as it buys fuel to generate power. At a higher discount rate, those future fuel bills also have a lower present value, which partly cushions the effect on project economics. The difference therefore depends on when costs occur and how much capital must be financed. Capital-intensive fossil projects can be highly rate-sensitive too.
